summary.text: The Big Rip is a hypothetical fate in which expansion progressively tears apart everything from stars and galaxies to atoms, until all particles are infinitely far apart.
It is only possible if the universe contains phantom energy, a hypothetical dark energy whose density increases as the universe expands.
Current data cannot rule it out, because uncertainties in measuring the key value w are still too large to separate the possible cases.

facts.label: Key value
facts.value: The equation of state parameter w

facts.label: Phantom energy
facts.value: Has w below -1, so its density grows with expansion

facts.label: Planck estimate
facts.value: w near -1.028, so the earliest rip is about 200 billion years away

facts.label: Planets break free
facts.value: Planetary systems come unbound about three months before the end

items.prompt: Suppose w sits between -1 and 0. The expansion accelerates, but dark energy fades over time. What does that mean for the Big Rip?

options.label: It happens, but much later than expected
It happens only for the smallest structures
It does not happen
It happens once the dark energy fully fades

items.explain: If w is between -1 and 0, the dark energy tends to dissipate over time and the Big Rip does not happen.

items.prompt: In the Big Rip, the horizon becomes smaller than a structure. What happens to that structure?

options.label: No force can act between its far parts, so it is ripped apart
Its gravity grows stronger and holds it together
It shrinks along with the horizon, staying intact
Only its outermost layer is pulled away

items.explain: When the horizon is smaller than a structure, no interaction by any fundamental force can occur between its most remote parts.

items.prompt: In the example with w of -1.5, which event comes earliest?

options.label: Planets fly off from their stars
Stars and planets are torn apart
Atoms are ionized and destroyed
Galaxies are separated from each other

items.explain: In that example, galaxies separate about 200 million years before the end, long before planetary systems unbind or atoms are destroyed.

items.prompt: In an accelerating universe dominated by a cosmological constant, bound structures effectively ignore the expansion. What would be different in the Big Rip?

options.label: The Hubble constant would drop to exactly zero
The Hubble constant would grow to infinity in a finite time
The Hubble constant would stay small and unchanging
The expansion would reverse into a contraction

items.explain: In the Big Rip the Hubble constant increases to infinity in a finite time, rather than staying small and unchanging.

items.prompt: Measurements put w extremely close to -1, but never exactly -1. Why can't scientists dismiss the Big Rip?

options.label: A value can be measured close to -1 but not at exactly -1
Any value near -1 guarantees that it will happen
Measurements of w are impossible to make at all
A value of exactly -1 would make it certain

items.explain: If w were exactly -1 the Big Rip could not happen, but w cannot be measured at exactly -1, so the Big Rip is very difficult to rule out.

items.prompt: A new measurement puts w even closer to -1, though still below it. What happens to the earliest possible date of the Big Rip?

options.label: It moves much closer to the present
It stays exactly where it was
It is pushed further into the future
It becomes impossible to calculate

items.explain: The closer w is to -1, the further the Big Rip is in the future.

paragraphs.heading: Torn apart by expansion
paragraphs.text: The Big Rip is a proposed ending for the universe in which expansion pulls everything apart, from galaxies and stars down to atoms and subatomic particles. By a definite moment in the future, every particle would be infinitely far from every other. At that final point, called a singularity, the observable universe would shrink to zero size while all distances grew without limit.

paragraphs.heading: Not the usual kind of expansion
paragraphs.text: In the standard model of cosmology, the expansion is speeding up and will become exponential once the cosmological constant dominates. That growth is the same over every equal stretch of time, and it comes with a small Hubble constant that never changes, which any bound material structure can effectively ignore. In a Big Rip, by contrast, the Hubble constant climbs to infinity in a finite time.

paragraphs.heading: Phantom energy
paragraphs.text: A Big Rip can only happen if the universe holds phantom energy, a proposed form of dark energy with implausible physical properties. The key number is the equation of state parameter, w, the ratio of dark energy's pressure to its energy density. If w lies between −1 and 0, the expansion speeds up but dark energy thins out over time, and there is no rip. Phantom energy has w below −1, so its density rises as the universe expands. If it keeps rising without limit, it could overcome every force that holds the universe together.

paragraphs.heading: How the tearing works
paragraphs.text: A universe ruled by phantom energy expands faster and faster. As it does, the cosmological event horizon, the distance within which objects can still affect an observer, keeps shrinking. Once that horizon is smaller than some structure, none of the fundamental forces can act between its farthest parts, and the structure is ripped apart.

paragraphs.heading: A countdown
paragraphs.text: A team led by Robert R. Caldwell of Dartmouth College worked out how long it would take to reach a Big Rip. Taking Ωₘ = 0.3, w = −1.5 and H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc as an example, they found the end would come about 22 billion years from now. Galaxies would be pulled away from each other about 200 million years before the end, and would start to fall apart about 60 million years before it. Systems of planets like ours would come loose about three months before. Stars and planets themselves would be shredded in the final minutes, and with just 10⁻¹⁹ seconds or so left, even atoms would be destroyed.

paragraphs.heading: Could it really happen
paragraphs.text: Recent studies point instead to steady expansion ending in heat death, because w = −1. If w were exactly −1, a Big Rip could not happen at all. But today's data are not yet precise enough to tell whether w is below, equal to or above −1. Data from the Planck mission put w at −1.028 (±0.031), which pushes the earliest possible rip to about 200 billion years away. Since measuring w as exactly −1 is nearly impossible, better measurements can push that date later but the Big Rip stays very hard to rule out completely.
